**Given:** The compact set $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, the smooth
amplitude $a$ supported in $K$ with $k\cdot a(k)=0$, the fixed SI laboratory
chart, and the fields defined above.

[F1] Schwartz space consists of actual smooth functions $f$ for which every
polynomially weighted derivative $x^\alpha\partial^\beta f$ is bounded; this
is the definition of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$.
([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]])

[F2] A potential pair obeys $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and
$B=\operatorname{curl}A$; its Coulomb condition is $\operatorname{div}A=0$.
([[def-em-gauge-transformation]])

[F3] The complex plane-wave encoding uses the componentwise real part of
$e\exp(i\theta)$; the real-part map is real-linear, $i^2=-1$, and
$\partial_z\exp z=\exp z$. The chain rule applies to the affine real phase
$k\cdot x-c|k|t$.
([[def-em-complex-plane-wave]],
[[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]],
[[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]],
[[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F4] The vacuum energy density is
$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|E|^2+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}|B|^2$, with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$.
([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])

[F5] Continuous real functions on closed nondegenerate rectangles are Riemann
integrable; the Riemann integral over a rectangle is the common lower and upper
Darboux value, and iterated integrals over product rectangles agree with the
multiple integral. A derivative integrates to its endpoint increment on a
closed interval, and the multidimensional integral obeys the absolute-value
estimate. ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]],
[[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]],
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]],
[[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]])

[F6] The fixed inertial laboratory chart uses the positively oriented
coordinates $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and time $t\in\mathbb R$; the electromagnetic
fields are real vector-valued maps on this region. In SI units, $c$ is the
vacuum speed, $[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[E]=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$,
$[A]=\mathrm{T\,m}$, and $[B]=\mathrm T$.
([[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]])

[F7] Divergence, curl, and partial derivatives have the stated component
formulas. For real $k$ and complex $a$, the cross-product identity
$k\times(k\times a)=k(k\cdot a)-|k|^2a$ follows by applying the real vector
triple-product lemma to the real and imaginary parts of $a$.
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cm-cross-product-triple-identity]])

[A1] The adopted smooth Maxwell branch is
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ for smooth fields and
continuous sources. This packet uses the source-free case $\rho=0$, $J=0$.
([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]])


 1.1 Since $K$ is compact and excludes $0$, it has positive distance from the origin. Thus extending $a$ by zero across a neighborhood of $0$ gives a smooth compactly supported map on all of $\mathbb R^3$. For any compact time interval $J$, each function $f_t(k):=a(k)\exp(-ic|k|t)$ and each of its $t$-derivatives is smooth and supported in $K$; all its derivatives are uniformly bounded on $K\times J$. Every integral in the Definition is therefore an ordinary Riemann integral of a continuous compactly supported function. Differentiating in $x$ or $t$ under the integral is justified because the corresponding difference quotients converge uniformly on $K$ for each fixed $(x,t)$: the phase derivatives in $(x,t)$ are bounded because $k$ ranges over $K$ and $t$ lies in $J$, while the complex exponential has unit modulus. The one-variable mean-value estimate for the exponential is therefore uniform in $k$. The absolute-integral estimate in [F5] then bounds the difference between the integrals by the volume of a containing cube times the uniform error, which tends to zero. Iterating this argument for the resulting derivatives proves existence and continuity of every mixed space-time derivative. [given, F3, F5, F6, construct]

2.1 For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, differentiating in $x$ multiplies the integrand by $(ik)^\beta$. To control a factor $x_j$, integrate the $k_j$-derivative of the product of the compactly supported factor and $\exp(ik\cdot x)$ over a containing cube. The one-dimensional FTC in [F5] gives zero boundary terms because the factor vanishes near both endpoints; Riemann-Fubini in [F5] integrates that identity over the other two coordinates. Repeating this argument transfers every monomial $x^\alpha$ to derivatives in $k$, leaving an integral of $\partial_k^\alpha((ik)^\beta f_t(k))$ times a unit-modulus exponential, up to the fixed factor of modulus one produced by integration by parts. Its absolute value is uniformly bounded in $x$ and locally uniformly in $t$. The same argument applies after any $t$-derivative, since it only adds the smooth factor $(-ic|k|)^q$ on $K$. By [F1], $A_+$, $A$, $E$, and $B$ are therefore Schwartz in $x$ at each $t$, with the claimed local bounds. [step 1.1, F1, F5, algebra]

3.1 Expanding $\prod_{j=1}^3(1+|x_j|)^2$ gives finitely many absolute monomials, each controlled by a Schwartz seminorm in [F1]. Hence each Schwartz component $h$ is bounded by $C_h\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-2}$. Applying this bound to $E$ and $B$ shows that $|E|^2$ and $|B|^2$ are bounded by a constant times $\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-4}$. Each one-dimensional factor has finite integral $\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|s|)^{-4}ds=2/3$; by Riemann-Fubini in [F5], the product bound is integrable on the increasing cubes. Formula [F4] therefore gives a finite box-exhaustion energy $W(t)$. [step 2.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

3.2 Put $\gamma:=(2\pi)^{-3/2}$. Direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}A=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int i(k\cdot a(k)) \exp(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t))\,d^3k=0$. The identity $\varphi=0$ and [F2] show that $(\varphi,A)$ represents exactly the displayed $(E,B)$ and is in Coulomb gauge. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, algebra]

3.3 Put $q(k,x,t):=\exp(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t))$ and $\gamma:=(2\pi)^{-3/2}$. By [F3] and real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$, $E=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int i c|k|a(k)q\,d^3k$ and $B=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int i(k\times a(k))q\,d^3k$. Differentiating each integrand using [F3], [F7], and step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{div}E=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int -c|k|(k\cdot a(k))q\,d^3k=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int -k\cdot(k\times a(k))q\,d^3k=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB =2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int[-c|k|k\times a(k)+c|k|k\times a(k)]q\,d^3k=0$, and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE =2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int[-k\times(k\times a(k))-|k|^2a(k)]q\,d^3k=0$. The last equality uses the cross-product identity in [F7] and $k\cdot a(k)=0$. These are the source-free equations in [A1], proving that the integrated fields satisfy the adopted smooth Maxwell branch. [step 1.1, step 2.1, A1, F3, F7, algebra]

4.1 The exponent $k\cdot x-c|k|t$ is dimensionless. Since $d^3k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, the assigned $[a]=\mathrm{T\,m^4}$ gives $[A]=\mathrm{T\,m}$; then $E=-\partial_tA$ has units $\mathrm{T\,m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ has units $\mathrm T$. These agree with [F6]. [F6, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Reals $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$.

[F1] The real numbers form a complete ordered field, and each nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root; a positive radicand has a positive root. [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] [[thm-of-square-roots]]

[F2] For real $t$, $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$, $|e^{it}|=1$, and $e^{i\pi}=-1$; complex modulus is the square root of the sum of squares of real and imaginary parts. Hence $|\cos t|\le1$, using order preservation by squaring on nonnegative reals. [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]

[F3] The complex exponential satisfies $e^{a+b}=e^ae^b$ for complex $a,b$. [[def-complex-exponential]] [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]

[F4] The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
derivatives $\cos$ and $-\sin$, and $\sin 0=0$. Every real $t$ is a limit point of $\mathbb R$:
for $\varepsilon>0$, $t+\varepsilon/2$ is a distinct point within distance
$\varepsilon$. Thus both functions are continuous on $\mathbb R$.
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]] [[def-limit-point-r]] [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]

[F5] If a real function is continuous on a closed nondegenerate interval and differentiable on its interior, its endpoint difference equals its derivative at some interior point times the interval length. [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]


 1.1 Rationalizing the definition of $R$ gives $R(s)=\bigl((1-s/2)^2-(1-s)\bigr)/(1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s}) =s^2/\bigl(4(1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s})\bigr)$. The denominator is positive because $s<1$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For real $a,b$, let $d:=a-b$. By [F3], $e^{ia}-e^{ib}=e^{ib}e^{id/2}(e^{id/2}-e^{-id/2})$; [F2] gives $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|=2|\sin(d/2)|$. If $d\ne0$, apply [F5] to $\sin$ on the interval with endpoints $0$ and $d/2$; [F2] gives $|\cos|\le1$, so [F4] yields $|\sin(d/2)|\le|d|/2$. The same inequality is immediate for $d=0$. Thus $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Put $t:=\sqrt{1-\delta^2}$, so $0<t\le1$. Since $1-s\ge1-\delta^2$, the nonnegative roots obey $\sqrt{1-s}\ge t$: otherwise the difference of their squares, factored as a product of a positive sum and positive difference, would give $1-s<1-\delta^2$. Hence $1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s}\ge1-\delta^2/2+t=(1+t)^2/2\ge2t^3$; the last inequality follows from $(1+t)^2\ge4t$ and $t\ge t^3$. Substitution into step 1.1 proves $0\le R(s)\le s^2/(8t^3)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $a:=zk_0\sqrt{1-s}$ and $b:=zk_0(1-s/2)$ in step 1.2. Then $|a-b|=|z|k_0R(s)$, so step 2.1 gives the stated multiplier bound. [given, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A fixed inertial chart, $c>0$, $\omega>0$, $0<\delta<1$, and
$u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with Fourier support in $D_\delta$.

[F1] The Schwartz Fourier convention is the displayed $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$
integral, and under countable choice it extends uniquely to a unitary map on
complex $L^2$; its inverse is the unitary inverse. [[thm-fourier-inversion-on-schwartz-space]] [[thm-plancherel]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F2] The laboratory chart has spatial coordinates in metres and time in seconds;
$c$ carries $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\omega$ carries $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. [[def-em-lab-geometry]] [[def-em-si-conventions]]

[A1] The adopted scalar aperture model takes a finite complex distribution on
a compact planar aperture and assigns an outgoing scalar Helmholtz field in a
polarization-insensitive regime; it does not assert exact Maxwell validity or
that every aperture output is band-limited or square-integrable on a plane.
[[post-em-scalar-aperture-model]]

[F3] The existing transverse Fourier-field definition uses a smooth compactly
supported three-dimensional wavevector amplitude supported away from zero and
imposes the bilinear condition $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a(\mathbf k)=0$; its
three-dimensional Schwartz-packet class is distinct from the present
two-dimensional fixed-frequency $L^2$ data. [[def-emx-transverse-fourier-field]]

[F4] A real plane-wave electric field is the componentwise real part of a
complex amplitude times $e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}$.
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]

[A2] The adopted smooth vacuum Maxwell branch includes
$\operatorname{div}E=0$ for source-free fields; it is a physical assumption,
not an empirical observation. [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]

[F5] Complex exponential and real-part operations are defined on every complex
number; the real-field encoding is componentwise. [[def-complex-exponential]] [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]

[F6] The real numbers are a complete ordered field. [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]

[F7] Every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root, and a
positive real has a positive root. [[thm-of-square-roots]]

[F8] Squaring preserves and reflects the order on nonnegative real numbers.
[[lem-of-square-monotone]]

[F9] For real $\theta$, $|e^{i\theta}|=1$; for $w=a+ib$,
$|\operatorname{Re}w|^2=a^2\le a^2+b^2=|w|^2$, hence
$|\operatorname{Re}w|\le|w|$. [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]

[F10] For real $a,b$, $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|$.
[[lem-emx-paraxial-phase-multiplier-bound]]


 1.1 For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, put $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$, $a:=k_0^2-|\mathbf q|^2$ and $b:=k_0^2(1-\delta^2)$. The support condition gives $0<b\le a\le k_0^2$. By [F6] and [F7] the roots in the definition exist; uniqueness and $k_0>0$ give $\sqrt b=k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}$ and $\sqrt{k_0^2}=k_0$. Applying [F8] to these nonnegative roots yields $0<k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\le k_z(\boldsymbol\xi)\le k_0$. [given, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 The transverse and axial coordinates are measured in metres, while $\mathbf q,k_z,k_0$ are in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$; thus every propagation-phase exponent is dimensionless. The multipliers preserve the unit of $u_0$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.3 [A1] fixes a separate scalar optical model, while the present Definition additionally restricts its plane data by $L^2$ and $D_\delta$ support; hence no existence or band-limit claim for every compact-aperture output is being made. [given, A1]

2.1 For $\boldsymbol\xi,\boldsymbol\eta\in D_\delta$, rationalizing gives $$|k_z(\boldsymbol\xi)-k_z(\boldsymbol\eta)|= \frac{\bigl||2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\eta|^2\bigr|} {k_z(\boldsymbol\xi)+k_z(\boldsymbol\eta)}.$$ The denominator is at least $2k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}>0$ by step 1.1, and the numerator is continuous in $(\boldsymbol\xi,\boldsymbol\eta)$; hence $k_z$ is continuous on $D_\delta$. Both real phase functions in the propagators are therefore continuous, so [F10] makes their exponential multipliers continuous and measurable. Each has modulus one by [F9]. [step 1.1, F9, F10, algebra]

3.1 Multiplication of $\mathcal F_2u_0$ by either measurable unit-modulus multiplier gives an $L^2$ class with the same norm; the unitary inverse in [F1] defines the unique propagated classes. For each fixed $t$, [F9] gives $|\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\omega t}u)|\le|e^{-i\omega t}u|=|u|$, so the real scalar fields are in $L^2$ and independent of the representative. [step 2.1, F1, F5, F9, algebra]

4.1 The fixed-frequency modes named above are not identified with the three-dimensional smooth Fourier packets of [F3]; their Maxwell constraint and the longitudinal estimate are established conditionally from the real field postulate and plane-wave convention in [F4] and [A2]. [given, F3, F4, A2] ∎

**Given:** $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, scalar data $u_0$ supported
in the angular cone, and an exact source-free monochromatic vacuum plane-wave
mode at $|\mathbf q|\le\delta k_0$.

[F1] The exact and paraxial fields are the $L^2$ Fourier multipliers
$e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)}$ and
$e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}$ on the support disk; the
$\mathcal F_2$ convention is $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. [[def-emx-angular-spectrum]]

[F2] Under countable choice, $\mathcal F_2$ is unitary on complex $L^2$ and
preserves its norm. [[thm-plancherel]] [[def-countable-choice]]

[F3] For $0\le s\le\delta^2$, the difference between phases
$zk_0\sqrt{1-s}$ and $zk_0(1-s/2)$ has multiplier modulus at most
$|z|k_0s^2/[8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}]$. [[lem-emx-paraxial-phase-multiplier-bound]]

[F4] A real plane wave is
$E(\mathbf x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf e e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)})$;
the exponential is differentiable and its phase derivative follows the chain
rule. [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]

[A1] In the smooth source-free vacuum branch, the adopted Maxwell equations
include $\operatorname{div}E=0$. [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]

[F5] For real $\theta$, $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ and
$e^{-i\pi/2}=-i$. [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]

[F6] Complex modulus is the Euclidean modulus of real and imaginary parts, and
the real transverse Euclidean norm is induced by the dot product; extend a real
dot product bilinearly when its second argument is complex. Order of squares
reflects order for nonnegative real numbers. [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]

[F7] In the fixed SI chart, $z$ is measured in metres, $k_0=\omega/c$ in
$\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, and $\delta$ is dimensionless. [[def-emx-angular-spectrum]] [[def-em-si-conventions]]


 1.1 On the Fourier support put $s:=|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/k_0^2$. Then $0\le s\le\delta^2$, $k_z=k_0\sqrt{1-s}$, and the paraxial axial phase is $k_0(1-s/2)$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Write $\phi(\mathbf x,t):=\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t$. For each spatial coordinate $x_j$, the chain rule and $\exp'=\exp$ in [F4] give $\partial_{x_j}E_j=\operatorname{Re}(iK_je_j e^{i\phi})$: indeed $\partial_{x_j}\phi=K_j$, and the real-part map commutes with this real derivative. Summing over $j=1,2,3$ and using additivity of real parts yields $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{Re}(i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf e)e^{i\phi})$. By [A1] this is zero for every $(\mathbf x,t)$. Put $S:=\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf e$. At $\mathbf x=0,t=0$, the expression is $\operatorname{Re}(iS)=-\operatorname{Im}S$, so $\operatorname{Im}S=0$. At $\mathbf x=0,t=\pi/(2\omega)$, [F5] gives $e^{i\phi}=-i$ and the expression is $\operatorname{Re}(S)$, so $\operatorname{Re}S=0$. Thus $S=0$, that is, $\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp+k_ze_z=0$. [given, F4, F5, A1, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], the difference of the two Fourier multipliers has modulus at most $C:=|z|k_0\delta^4/[8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}]$ throughout the support. Unitarity [F2] therefore gives $\|u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z)-u_{\mathrm{par}}(z)\|_2^2 =\int |\widehat u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)|^2 |e^{izk_z}-e^{ik_0z-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}|^2\,d^2\boldsymbol\xi \le C^2\|u_0\|_2^2$; taking nonnegative square roots proves the scalar bound. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 Since $k_z\ge k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}>0$, step 1.2 gives $|e_z|=|\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp|/k_z$. The identity $(|\mathbf q|^2|\mathbf e_\perp|^2-|\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp|^2) =|q_xe_y-q_ye_x|^2\ge0$ implies $|\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf e_\perp|\le|\mathbf q||\mathbf e_\perp|$; using $|\mathbf q|\le\delta k_0$ yields the displayed longitudinal bound. [step 1.2, F6, algebra]

3.1 The scalar error prefactor $|z|k_0\delta^4/[8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}]$ and the longitudinal prefactor $\delta/\sqrt{1-\delta^2}$ are dimensionless by [F7]; hence the two bounds have the same units as their respective field amplitudes. [F7, algebra] ∎



The scalar bound is conditional on the stated spectral support and its
longitudinal scale $|z|k_0\delta^4$. It does not claim a bound for arbitrary
aperture data or for exact vector Maxwell errors.

$e^{izk_0\sqrt{1-s}}$ and $e^{izk_0(1-s/2)}$, where

[F2] The exact remainder is

[F3] The Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ is unitary on complex $L^2$ under

[F4] Under countable choice, each nondegenerate box has Lebesgue measure equal

**Given:** Fix $k_0>0$ and choose one constant spectral norm
$A_\star>0$ (in volts for scalar fields measured in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$).

1.1 Set $\delta_n:=1/(n+2)$ and $R_n:=\delta_n k_0/(2\pi)$. Let $\Xi_n:=[R_n(1-\delta_n/4),R_n(1-\delta_n/8)] \times[0,R_n\delta_n/8]$. Its side lengths are both $R_n\delta_n/8>0$, so [F4] gives $0<|\Xi_n|=R_n^2\delta_n^2/64<\infty$. Define $\widehat u_{0,n}:=A_\star|\Xi_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf 1_{\Xi_n}$; then $\|\widehat u_{0,n}\|_2=A_\star$. For $\mathbf q=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ with $\boldsymbol\xi\in\Xi_n$, $q_x\ge\delta_n k_0(1-\delta_n/4)>\delta_n k_0(1-\delta_n)$ and $|\mathbf q|^2\le\delta_n^2k_0^2[(1-\delta_n/8)^2+(\delta_n/8)^2] \le\delta_n^2k_0^2$; hence this nonzero spectrum lies in the angular cone and concentrates near its outer radius. [given, F4, algebra]
